title: An Audit Requests Your GRC Artifacts
context: An external auditor asks to see how your organization documents its security requirements. You must present the right artifacts and explain their role.

n1.text: The auditor asks: "Which document states management's intent regarding acceptable use of resources?"

choices.text: The Acceptable Use Policy (AUP), approved by management
choices.why: A policy conveys general intent and derives its authority from executive approval.
A runbook describes technical steps, not governance intent.
A baseline is a configuration standard, subordinate to policy.

n2.text: The auditor next asks for the verifiable technical rule that derives from it. What do you present?

choices.text: An encryption standard with a measurable minimum level
choices.why: A standard turns intent into a measurable requirement verifiable in an audit.
An advisory is a guideline: it recommends without mandating.
A BCP organizes recovery; it does not set a day-to-day technical rule.

n3.text: Final question: how do you prove these documents are maintained and enforced?

choices.text: Named owner, approval, distribution with acknowledgment, and dated reviews
choices.why: This is the complete lifecycle of a GRC artifact: authority, distribution, proof, and currency.

choices.text: The files are on the intranet, that is enough
choices.why: Publication alone proves neither approval, nor reading, nor review.

choices.text: The documents are very long and detailed
choices.why: Length is not proof of governance.

n4.outcome: You presented a coherent pyramid: approved policy, measurable standard, and proof of distribution and review.

debrief: Policy states intent and receives its authority from executive approval.
Standard converts intent into a measurable requirement; procedure describes the steps.
A credible GRC artifact has an owner, an approval date, and a review history.
